newsitem.title: USA: More than strong economy needed to cut deficit-Raines.
newsitem.headline: More than strong economy needed to cut deficit-Raines.

text.p: Wiping out the U.S. budget deficit requires more than a strong economy, White House Budget Director Franklin Raines said Wednesday in making a pitch to move forward with the balanced-budget agreement.
"The economy is not going to perform so much better that it's going to balance the budget by itself," Raines said.

Wall Street expectations that the budget deficit could fall to below $50 billion at the end of the 1997 fiscal year which ends Sept. 30 raised some questions about the need to move ahead with the balanced-budget agreement.
Congressional leaders and the White House reached the budget pact in May to eliminate the deficit by 2002.

Raines said he expected the deficit to improve this year, but would not give a specific projection. He called "absurd" some notions that letting current fiscal policy continue on "automatic pilot" would be better for eliminating the deficit than implementing the budget agreement.
"The budget agreement is necessary to balance the budget," he told reporters.

The economy was performing "very well" but in the next few years was not expected to be as strong as in 1997 or 1996, Raines said. "Our economic assumptions that we've been using show moderate economic growth over the next five years, and that moderate growth would be not as strong as the growth that we've had this year or last year," he said.

The U.S. economy surged ahead at a 5.9 pct annual growth rate in the first quarter this year but is forecast to slow to about a 2-to-2-1/2 percent pace in the second quarter. A stronger economy generally leads to higher tax revenues sent to the Treasury Department and reduces the deficit.
Robert Reischauer a senior fellow at Brookings Institution said a fiscal 1997 year-end deficit of $35 billion to $55 billion would not be surprising.

"I think the fact of the matter is that this budget agreement is not primarily about deficit reduction, the goal of this budget agreement was to achieve a balanced budget by 2002, but that's not a very high bar to clear," he said.
The main reason behind the agreement was more to provide a tax cut, reduce Medicare spending, and offer a "little bit" of net deficit reduction, Reischauer said.
Raines said he hoped members of Congress who have opposed moving ahead with the budget agreement not gain leverage.

He also said President Clinton would not sign a tax bill that would explode the deficit in later years, and added that currently there were provisions in both Senate and House bills that would do that.
House and Senate tax negotiators are trying to work out differences in their legislation to craft one final tax cut bill to send to the full Congress for a vote before the August recess.

A bipartisan group of Senate moderates met with top White House officials, including chief of staff Erskine Bowles, to discuss controversial proposals to gradually raise the Medicare eligibility age to 67 from 65 and make affluent seniors pay higher premiums for doctor's care.
President Clinton has said he might be able to support some form of Medicare income testing, but worries that raising the eligibility age would increase the ranks of the uinsured.

Nebraska Democratic Sen. Robert Kerrey said the group hoped to develop compromise proposals in the next 24 hours. One option would be to allow seniors to voluntarily buy into Medicare if the retirement age were raised.
